Repository: re-cinq/HALEngine
Ticket: #144 Deliver a user's conversation list over the WebSocket protocol

You are editing files in a git repository, mid-way through a ticket that
is already defined by RED acceptance tests. You perform exactly ONE
red-green-refactor round and then stop. Not two. Not "while I'm here".

The ticket's branch is checked out with write access at /var/tmp/loop-bench/runs/fef7690a21ee/workspace/target.
Run every command from inside it (`cd /var/tmp/loop-bench/runs/fef7690a21ee/workspace/target` first). The ticket
is at `/var/tmp/loop-bench/runs/fef7690a21ee/workspace/ticket.md`: read it before anything else. Pass `repo` (the
owner/name your task names above) on every `lore_*` call: the gateway has
no checkout to detect it from.

START by reading `.lore/dod.md` on this branch. Its "Done when these pass"
list is the bar; its Facets checklist is where the last round got to. It
names the strategy, the
acceptance tests that define done, and the facets expected. It is the
brief; the ticket below is the context.

RUN ONLY THE TEST YOU WRITE THIS ROUND, by its file, from the package
that owns it, with a deadline — for example `cd <package> && timeout 300 npx
vitest run <file>`. Never run the acceptance tests `.lore/dod.md` lists, nor a
directory that holds them: CI is the judge of this branch, runs them on
every push, and tells you where they stand. Read that from
`/var/tmp/loop-bench/runs/fef7690a21ee/workspace/round-brief.md` when it exists, or ask `lore_get_ci_failures`
— not from your memory, and not from what `.lore/dod.md` predicted. Not
the repository's full suite either, not lint, not the typechecker, not
the formatter. The pod's Bash hook refuses an acceptance test by name and
a runner given no test file.

If this pod cannot run your test — the command that runs it (`java`, `mvn`,
`gradle`, `go`, `cargo`, `dotnet`) is not found, or a wrapper such as
`./mvnw` reports no `JAVA_HOME` — do not look for it and do not install
it: no `sudo`, no `apt`, no `find /`, no download. Do the round from the
code, the tests and CI's verdict, commit and push; CI judges the push,
and a red build comes back to the next round as its brief. Say in your
final message that the round ran no tests here.

YOUR ROUND is the `tdd-loop` skill's three phases, in order, no steps
skipped: one failing test for the smallest facet that moves an acceptance
test closer to green, then the least code that passes it, then refactor
with the bar green. Never edit an acceptance test to make it pass — if an
acceptance test is wrong, stop and say so; that is a failed round.

Under `parallel-change`, all of this happens in the NEW module: leave the
old code alone and working until the acceptance tests are green, and make
the caller switch its own round. Under `characterize`, the
characterization tests are part of the green bar you must keep — a
refactor that reddens them is a behaviour change. Under `mechanical`,
there is no red phase at all: perform the exact edits its Facets
record and commit; the EXISTING tests `.lore/dod.md` names are CI's to
run, and its verdict says whether they stayed green. The diff is the
deliverable, and a round that invents a new test for it has left the
strategy.

Never add a test whose assertion subject is the repo's own source text —
readFileSync of a src/ or test file, a regex over another test,
counting a literal across files. That pins prose, not behaviour: where
prose must agree with a value, make the prose compute the value instead.

TRACEABILITY:
- Each test validates a statement in a spec or ADR. Add the inline
  parenthetical on that statement in the repository's established form —
  `Statement. ([validated by name](path/to/test.ts#L42))`. Inserting a
  test shifts every #Lnn link below it: when the repository has
  `scripts/spec-links/reanchor.mjs`, run
  `node scripts/spec-links/reanchor.mjs` from the repository root after
  the formatter — it moves each link to its test's current line, by test
  title, and prints the links it could not map, which you fix by hand.
  Without it, re-verify every existing #Lnn link on the statements you
  touch yourself.
- Stamp the test's spec anchor (the "specs/<path>#<ordinal>" it
  validates) so the repo's tests.list surfaces it as the descriptor's
  `spec` field and the VALIDATED_BY link is established automatically —
  see `.lore/test-commands.yml` for how this repo exposes descriptors.

- If this round completes what a `specs/<name>/spec.md` describes, update
  that spec's `| Status |` header row in the same branch (Draft ->
  Implemented/Shipped) so the status never lags the code.

BEFORE YOU EDIT A SYMBOL, ask the graph which tests already cover it:
`lore-query-trace` with `tests_covering` set to the file you are about to
change, and `ranges` as `start-end` when you know the span. The rows name
test FILES, because coverage is recorded per file, and they describe the
repository as main last projected it.

Main is the right coordinate for this question: a REGRESSION is by
definition a test that existed before your branch. That list is what tells
a red test apart from one. When CI's verdict on your last push names a
red test you did not write and the acceptance list does not hold, it is
a regression YOU caused — stop, fix the
code, and never "fix" the test. Say in your final message how many red
tests were yours and how many were regressions.

RULES:
- Do not fix unrelated smells you notice. Name them in your final message;
  act on none of them.
- Keep `.lore/dod.md` current: TICK the box of the facet you closed
  (`- [ ]` becomes `- [x]`) and append any new facet you discovered as an
  unchecked one. It is a live checklist, not an append-only log, and the
  next round reads it to see where the ticket actually stands.
- Commit when the test YOU wrote is green. Acceptance tests may still be
  red — that is the ordinary state mid-ticket, and the next round takes
  the next facet.
- If `/var/tmp/loop-bench/runs/fef7690a21ee/workspace/round-brief.md` exists, read it before `.lore/dod.md`. Its
  `The previous round reported` section is where the last round stopped.
  Its `CI reported failures` section is the verdict
  on the previous push, and it outranks `.lore/dod.md`: a red build means
  the ticket is NOT done, however many facets are ticked. Every finding
  it lists — each `path:line message` — is work this round owes before
  anything else. Fix ALL of them in this visit, format, push; there is no
  local re-run here that would show you the rest, and each finding you
  leave costs the ticket a pod and a CI cycle. Run 2a291314 spent two
  rounds reading a ticked dod.md and reporting "nothing left" under a
  verdict naming three lines; the guard sent it to repair each time. Do
  not re-run the whole build to find the failures; the section names them.

DELIVERY, NON-NEGOTIABLE — the next step runs in a DIFFERENT container:
- Before you commit, run the repository's FORMATTER over the files you
  changed (`npx prettier --write <files>`, `gofmt -w <files>`, whichever
  this repo uses) and nothing else from CI's checklist. Do NOT run the
  linter in this pod: CI runs it on every push, and here it does not
  fit — in this repository a two-file `eslint` peaks near 800 MB against
  a 1Gi pod, and runs 112256d9 and 62c1ca5e were OOM-killed on exactly
  that. A lint finding comes back as a red build naming the file and
  line, which the next round fixes with an editor.
- Do NOT typecheck here either. A green test is not a compiled build —
  vitest transpiles each file without checking types — but CI's build
  step is what proves it, and in this repository `tsc --noEmit` on
  `libs/shared` peaks near 950 MB against the 1Gi pod: run 2a291314's
  dod pod was OOM-killed on it. A type error comes back as a red build
  whose failed step and log tail name the file and line; the next
  round fixes it there. Read your imports and signatures twice instead.
- NEVER run a workspace build in this pod (`npm run build`, `tsc -b`, a
  `tsc` without `--noEmit`): tests resolve every workspace package from
  SOURCE, so nothing needs building for a test to see your change, and
  the build is the 950 MB step that OOM-killed run abac6ee9 while it
  rebuilt libs/shared for a test that never needed it.
- When the work is done, `git -C /var/tmp/loop-bench/runs/fef7690a21ee/workspace/target add` what you changed and commit it with a
  short, factual message. Then `git -C /var/tmp/loop-bench/runs/fef7690a21ee/workspace/target push origin HEAD`. The clone carries
  its own credentials, so a plain push authenticates; you need no token
  and must never look for one.
- Then bring the branch up to date with its base — `git fetch origin main`
  and merge `origin/main` in — and push again if that produced anything.
  A branch that cannot merge cleanly gets NO CI AT ALL: GitHub runs no
  workflow on a conflicted pull request, so the ticket parks on a build
  that will never start. Resolve any conflict now, favouring `origin/main`
  for anything this ticket did not write, and never by discarding your own
  work. This is why a nine-day-old branch stalled: 186 commits of drift,
  no checks, and a wait with nothing to wait for.
- Confirm it landed: `git status` must report the branch is not ahead of
  its upstream. An unpushed commit lives only in this container and
  dies with it — do NOT report success for one.
- If you genuinely changed nothing, say why — and read the result lines
  below before you choose one: "nothing left to write" and "I am stuck"
  are different endings here, and only the second is a failure.
- Do not open a pull request: you have no `gh` and no GitHub token. Lore
  opens the PR from the branch you push.

THE LAST LINE YOU PRINT is how the round ends. Print exactly one, on its
own line, as the final thing in your message. You are NOT deciding whether
the ticket is done — the build decides that, after your push. You are
reporting whether this round delivered anything.
- You committed and pushed a round:
  LORE_NODE_RESULT: {"outcome":"success","extras":{"tdd_done":"<the facet you closed>","tdd_next":"<the facet the next round takes, or 'acceptance green'>"}}
  This is the ordinary outcome, whether or not acceptance tests remain
  red. CI reads the branch next and sends you back if there is more.
- You wrote nothing because there was nothing left to write — every facet
  in `.lore/dod.md` is closed, its acceptance tests pass, AND no
  `CI reported failures` section is in the round brief (a red verdict IS something
  left to write; fix its findings and report the line above instead):
  LORE_NODE_RESULT: {"outcome":"success","extras":{"tdd_next":"acceptance green"}}
  SUCCESS, not failure. The branch is already pushed; the build judges it
  next, and a green one sends the ticket to review. Reporting failure for
  a round that found the work already done ENDS THE TICKET and strands its
  work on an open branch — which is exactly how run ae788c93 died with the
  implementation complete and all four facets checked off.
- You cannot name a next facet, or the bar will not go green: say exactly
  what blocks you, then:
  LORE_NODE_RESULT: {"outcome":"failed","extras":{"tdd_blocked":"<one line: what blocks you>"}}
  "This is hard" is not stuck; "there is no facet I can express as a test"
  is. Report failure when you are STUCK, never when you are FINISHED.

# Definition of Done

> #143 gives a consumer `store.listFor(userId)` inside the server process. The client on the other end of the WebSocket has no way to ask for it, and the consumer who wants a conversation picker without standing up their own REST endpoint has to write one anyway.

**Strategy: `direct`** — `createServer` and the WebSocket upgrade/message pipeline already exist and accept frames over a real WebSocket connection, so acceptance tests can connect today, send `list_sessions` frames, and fail directly on the missing `session_list` and `list_sessions` validation/dispatch behaviour.

## Done when these pass

- [ ] **listing conversations over the WebSocket protocol › answers list_sessions for the authenticated user with ISO dates, forwarding limit and before while ignoring any client userId** — Sends `{type: 'list_sessions', limit, before, userId}` over a connected WebSocket and verifies `store.listFor` is called with the socket's authenticated `userId` (`session.userId`) and `{limit, before}`, answering `{type: 'session_list', sessions}` with `createdAt` and `updatedAt` serialised as ISO-8601 strings.
      `src/transport/conversationList.acceptance.test.ts`

- [ ] **listing conversations over the WebSocket protocol › answers an empty session_list when the store has no listFor, and SERVER_ERROR with a ws error log when listFor throws** — Verifies that a store without `listFor` answers `{type: 'session_list', sessions: []}` and a store whose `listFor` throws/rejects logs an error under category `'ws'` with the userId and error message and answers `{type: 'error', code: 'SERVER_ERROR'}`.
      `src/transport/conversationList.acceptance.test.ts`

- [ ] **listing conversations over the WebSocket protocol › accepts a bare list_sessions frame and rejects a malformed limit or before with INVALID_MESSAGE without calling listFor** — Verifies that `{type: 'list_sessions'}` is accepted while non-integer or negative `limit` values and malformed `before` cursors (`sessionId` outside 1–128 chars or unparseable `updatedAt`) are rejected with `INVALID_MESSAGE` without invoking `store.listFor`.
      `src/transport/conversationList.acceptance.test.ts`

## Facets

- [x] Add `ListSessionsMessage`, `SessionSummaryFrame`, and `SessionListMessage` to `src/types/messages.ts`, include them in `IncomingMessage` and `OutgoingMessage`, and re-export them from `src/index.ts`.
- [x] Validate `list_sessions` frames in `src/transport/ws/validation.ts` (optional non-negative integer `limit`; optional `before` object with 1–128 char `sessionId` and finite-date `updatedAt` string or number; strip unknown fields like `userId`).
- [x] Thread `sessionStore` into `createMessageHandler` (optional parameter so existing 1-arg and 2-arg callers keep working) and wire it in `src/transport/createServer.ts`.
- [x] Handle `list_sessions` in `src/transport/ws/messageHandler.ts` (and helper in `src/transport/ws/sender.ts` if needed) by reading `session.userId`, calling `await sessionStore?.listFor?.(session.userId, {limit, before})`, serialising `Date` fields to ISO strings, and on error logging via `log.error('ws', ...)` and sending `ErrorCodes.SERVER_ERROR`.
- [x] Document `list_sessions` and `session_list` in `specs/hal-engine-websocket-protocol/spec.md` and `specs/hal-engine-conversation-list/spec.md`.
- [x] Add `history?: {enabled: boolean}` to `HalEngineConfig.transport` and `HalServerOptions`, threaded into `createServer`. With it off, `list_sessions` should answer with an `error` frame (`UNSUPPORTED`) and no list.
- [x] Add `§ Conversation list` to `docs/getting-started.md` by editing `example/full-config.ts` and running `npm run docs:fix`.

## Out of scope

- Conversation titles or previews (first user message, model-generated title).
- Deleting or renaming a conversation from the client over the socket.
- Switching the socket's active session in place (`?sessionId=` on reconnect is how a conversation is rejoined).
- Holding pagination cursor state server-side (the client pages with `before`).
- An operator view of another user's conversations or live sync between open tabs.
# Deliver a user's conversation list over the WebSocket protocol

Issue: re-cinq/HALEngine#144
Labels: type:feature, size:M, area:api, area:compliance, epic:extension-points

Part of #35

## Why

#143 gives a consumer `store.listFor(userId)`.
It does not give a **client** anything: the browser holding the socket cannot reach the store, so
every consumer that wants a history sidebar has to stand up its own authenticated HTTP route over
the same data the engine already authenticated on the upgrade. That is a second authorisation
path to the same personal data, written once per consumer, each one able to get the ownership
check wrong in its own way — the exact failure #45 went out of its way to avoid for resume.

A consumer may have no such route to extend: an engine deployment behind an api with a session
store and no conversation endpoints of its own has nothing to add this to. The engine already knows who is connected and already
replays a conversation on resume; answering "which conversations do I have" over the same socket
is the smaller surface.

## What to do

- `src/types/messages.ts`, additive only:
  - `ListConversationsMessage {type: 'list_conversations'; limit?: number; before?: string}` into
    `IncomingMessage`. There is no user id field, and that is the point: the list is always the
    connection's authenticated user's.
  - `ConversationListMessage {type: 'conversation_list'; conversations: ConversationSummary[]}`
    into `OutgoingMessage`, where `ConversationSummary` is `SessionSummary` with its two times as
    ISO strings — `Date` does not survive `JSON.stringify` as a `Date`, and the protocol types
    describe what goes on the wire.
- `validation.ts`: a `list_conversations` case — `limit`, when present, an integer 1–200;
  `before`, when present, a string `Date.parse` accepts. Anything else is `INVALID_MESSAGE`, as
  the two existing cases do it.
- Handling: `createMessageHandler` takes the session store and the new options alongside the
  orchestrator (`createServer` already holds both), and answers `list_conversations` on the
  non-locked path beside `ping` — a history request is not a turn and must not queue behind a
  streaming answer.
- The user id comes from `ws.userId`, never from the frame. Add the regression:
  a frame carrying an extra `userId` of another user is answered with the connecting user's own
  list.
- Opt-in: `HalEngineConfig.transport.history?: {enabled: boolean}`, default off, threaded through
  `createServer`'s options like `resume`. With it off, `list_conversations` is answered with an
  `error` frame and no list.
- A store that implements no `listFor` is answered with an `error`, not an empty list: a client
  that renders "no conversations" for a user who has several is a worse answer than one that
  renders a failure. `ErrorCodes` gains one code for both cases (`UNSUPPORTED`), additive.
- Picking a conversation needs nothing new: the client reconnects with `?sessionId=<id>`, which
  #45 already ships with the ownership check and the replay. No in-band switch frame, no second
  replay path.
- Specs and docs: extend `specs/hal-engine-websocket-protocol/spec.md` (the two frames, their
  field tables, the authorisation rule) and the conversation-list spec; add § Conversation list
  to `docs/getting-started.md` by editing `example/full-config.ts` and running `npm run docs:fix`
  — that listing sits under `<!-- doc-block: example/full-config.ts#full-config -->` and
  `npm run docs:check` fails a hand-edited block.

## Decisions

- **A frame, not a REST route.** The REST chat routes are demo-only and are not where a consumer is meant to build. The WebSocket is where the caller is
  already authenticated, once per connection, by the consumer's own `wsAuth`.
- **Its own opt-in flag, separate from `resume`.** Resume hands a client back a conversation it
  was already in; a list tells it what else the user has. A deployer who turned on resume did not
  thereby agree to the second disclosure, and a config that conflates them cannot be audited.
- **Answered off the per-session lock.** `PerSessionLock` serialises turns (#47). A list request
  that queued behind a two-minute streaming answer would look broken, and it mutates nothing.
- **An error, not an empty list, when it cannot be answered.** See above; silence that looks like
  data is the one failure mode a history view cannot recover from.
- **Answered when asked, never pushed.** No `conversation_list` arrives unsolicited: a client
  that just started a conversation knows, and a push would need a fan-out across the sockets a
  resumed session can be open on.
- **The frame is accepted by `validateMessage` whether or not the feature is on**, and the
  handler is what refuses it. Validation is static and has no config; the alternative is
  threading options into a pure validator to turn a type into "unknown".

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `src/types/messages.ts` gains only new interfaces and their two union members (**amended:** four interfaces, not two — each frame needs a type for its own payload, `ConversationCursor` for what a client sends back and `ConversationSummary` for a row on the wire) — a
      `git diff` of that file touches no existing line, and a fixture pins that every message
      literal valid before this change still compiles
- [ ] `validateMessage({type: 'list_conversations'})` is valid; with `limit: 0`, `limit: 201`,
      `limit: 1.5`, `limit: '10'` or `before: 'not a date'` it is invalid with a message naming
      the field
- [ ] With `history: {enabled: true}` and a store holding three conversations for the user, a
      `list_conversations` frame is answered with exactly one `conversation_list` carrying three
      summaries, newest first, each `createdAt` and `updatedAt` an ISO string, and no
      `stream_end`
- [ ] A frame carrying `{type: 'list_conversations', userId: '<another user>'}` is answered with
      the connecting user's own list, and the store's `listFor` is called with `ws.userId` —
      asserted on the recorded argument, not only on the frame
- [ ] `limit` and `before` reach `listFor` as the frame sent them. **Amended:** `before` is a
      `{updatedAt, sessionId}` cursor of ISO strings, not a `Date`. This was written before
      #143's review found that paging on a timestamp alone drops a conversation whenever two
      share an activity time, so the store's cursor became a composite that accepts an ISO
      string; a `Date` cannot carry the tie-break. The handler passes `{limit, before}` with
      both possibly `undefined` rather than omitting the argument, which is the same call
- [ ] With `history` absent, the same frame is answered with one `error` frame whose code is
      `UNSUPPORTED` and no `conversation_list`
- [ ] With `history: {enabled: true}` against a store implementing no `listFor`, the answer is
      the same `error` frame, and `grep` shows no code path that sends `conversations: []`
- [ ] A `listFor` that rejects is answered with one `error` frame whose code is `SERVER_ERROR`
      and whose message carries no store detail, the socket stays open, and the failure is
      logged with the session id and no user content. **Added during the build:** a store throwing
      the new exported `StoreCannotList` is answered `UNSUPPORTED` instead, so an injected
      collection without a `find` reads as the misconfiguration it is rather than a database
      that failed
- [ ] A `list_conversations` sent while a `user_message` is streaming on the same session is
      answered before that turn's `stream_end` — it does not wait on the lock
- [ ] A client that takes an id from a `conversation_list` and reconnects with `?sessionId=<id>`
      receives `resumed: true` and that conversation's replay, with no new transport code: the
      test exercises the existing #45 path end to end
- [ ] `ConnectedMessage` is unchanged by this issue
- [ ] **GDPR.** The protocol spec states that `conversation_list` carries one authenticated
      user's own conversation metadata and no conversation content, that the user id is taken
      from the connection and never from the frame, and that `transport.history` is the
      deployer's decision to make a user's history reachable from the client; `SessionResumeOptions`'
      retention note is mirrored on the new options type, pointing at #41
- [ ] `CHANGELOG.md` carries an entry under `## [Unreleased]` written for somebody installing the
      package
- [ ] The `docs/getting-started.md` change is made in `example/full-config.ts` and the doc
      regenerated with `npm run docs:fix`, not typed into the markdown
- [ ] Spec statements carry trailing `([validated by: ...](...#Lnn))` citations, `Status` rows
      match coverage, and `npm run check:spec-links`, `npm run check:spec-status` and
      `npm run spec:names` pass
- [ ] The version bump is MINOR — new optional config, two additive protocol frames, one new
      error code — and the PR body says so; no migration guide is owed
- [ ] `npm run verify` passes and the coverage floors for the touched groups hold or rise

## Amendments

Three things changed between writing this issue and building it, each marked in the criterion it
affects:

1. **`before` is a cursor, not a timestamp.** #143's review found that paging on `updatedAt` alone
   silently drops a conversation when two share an activity time. The store's cursor became
   `{updatedAt, sessionId}`, so the frame carries both halves and the validator refuses one half
   alone. Built as originally written, the transport would have reintroduced the defect the store
   had just been fixed for.
2. **`messages.ts` gains four interfaces, not two** — the two frames plus the two payload types
   they describe.
3. **`StoreCannotList` is new public surface**, beyond what this issue specified: without it a
   permanent store misconfiguration cannot be told from a transient failure, in either the client
   frame or the log.

Two decisions the criteria did not anticipate:

- **`transport.history` without `transport.resume` is useless, and now says so.** `?sessionId=` is
  read only when resume is enabled, so a list whose rows cannot be opened is a deployment slip:
  the engine warns at startup and the documentation says so where it tells a client to reconnect
  with a row's id. Refusing to start was considered and rejected as too blunt for a library.
- **The conversation the connection is in is listed like any other**, so a fresh connect sees a row
  of its own holding no entries. Filtering it out was rejected: it is a real conversation the user
  is in, and it is their newest the moment they send anything.

## Tech notes

Depends on #143: without `listFor` there is
nothing to send.

Key paths: `src/types/messages.ts`, `src/types/session.ts` (`ErrorCodes`),
`src/transport/ws/{validation,messageHandler,sender}.ts`, `src/transport/createServer.ts`,
`src/config.ts`, `example/full-config.ts`, `specs/hal-engine-websocket-protocol/spec.md`.

Out of scope: a preview or title on the summaries (its own issue); deleting a conversation from
the client, which would put an erasure primitive on the wire and needs its own authorisation
decision; paging state held server-side — the client pages with `before`; an operator view of
another user's conversations, which is an authorisation question of its own; and live sync between open tabs,
which #124 ruled out.

Refs #143, #145, #41, #45, #47, #124

# ADR-006: Four re-lint rules suppressed where they misread the domain

This ADR records four inline suppressions of `@re-cinq/eslint-plugin-re-lint` rules, and why each is a mismatch between a good rule and this repo's domain rather than debt to be paid down. Every other finding the rules report stays reported: three of the four rules remain enabled and still fire elsewhere in the tree, and the suppressions are per-site with a reason attached, never a rule switched off repo-wide. The alternative in each case was to change working code in a direction that made it worse - a breaking public API change, an eagerly-loaded SDK, a lost type narrowing at a trust boundary, and a deleted regression pin. This decision is implemented.

## Context

`eslint.config.mjs` enables 31 of re-lint's 39 rules, several of which other adopters decline. Enabling them was deliberate: the instruction was to integrate every applicable linter and let it fail rather than refactor to suit it, so the backlog would be visible. Working through that backlog separates cleanly into findings whose fix improves the code and findings whose fix does not. These four are the second kind. They were identified while clearing the mechanical findings, each verified by reading the rule's own source or probing it, not inferred from the message text.

## Decision

Five sites carry `eslint-disable-next-line` (or, in one case, a file-level `eslint-disable`) with a `--` reason referring here, under the four decisions below. Together they account for every finding these three rules report: run with `--no-inline-config` and the count is three `no-flag-params`, one `prefer-polymorphism` and one `test-imports-its-subject`. The sixth was withdrawn when its rule stopped firing - see the `validateMessage` entry.

**`re-lint/no-flag-params` on `AIError`'s `retryable` parameter** (`src/types/ai.ts`). `AIError` is exported from `src/index.ts` and `retryable` is a `public readonly` constructor parameter, so it is part of the published API. The rule's remedy - split the function into two named functions - means two error classes or two factories, which is a breaking change for every consumer constructing an `AIError`. CLAUDE.md routes breaking changes through an issue, a migration guide, a MINOR bump and a deprecation period; a lint sweep is not that process.

The same constraint reaches every other site that constructs a retryable `AIError`, because `retryable` defaults to `false` and there is no other way to express one. Two carry the same suppression: `mapVertexError` in `src/providers/vertex/vertexProvider.ts`, which classifies a rate limit, and one call site in `src/transport/ws/messageHandler.test.ts`, which builds the error a handler is expected to surface. In both the rule's premise is false in the same way - the boolean is not selecting a behaviour, it is a field of a value.

Two further sites in `src/providers/vertex/vertexProvider.test.ts` carried this suppression until those tests stopped constructing an expected `AIError` at all. Asserting on the thrown error's `name`, `code` and `retryable` fields is both stricter and free of the literal: `expect(...).rejects.toThrow(new AIError(msg, code, true))` compares only the message, so it passed against a deliberately mis-classified error.

**`re-lint/prefer-polymorphism` on `createProvider`** (`src/providers/providerFactory.ts`). The five-way `switch` on `config.type` narrows a discriminated union onto five factories that take five different config types. A lookup table keyed by the string loses that narrowing: TypeScript cannot prove the selected arm's parameter matches the value being dispatched, so the table needs a cast at exactly the point the union was buying safety. This is the same premise as the `validateMessage` entry below, and it is not the premise this entry carried before the ESM conversion. Until then each arm `require`d its provider's module lazily and the suppression was justified as a loading boundary - but `src/index.ts` statically re-exports all five factories, so the factory's laziness never prevented a single module load. The boundary that does work lives inside each provider, around the vendor SDK, and stays there.

**`re-lint/prefer-polymorphism` on `validateMessage`** (`src/transport/ws/validation.ts`). Withdrawn, not reversed. The `switch` on `message.type` narrows an untrusted WebSocket frame through a discriminated union, and a lookup keyed by string would lose that narrowing at precisely the point where the input is attacker-controlled and the type is a claim rather than a fact. The `default` arm rejecting unknown types is the security behaviour. But removing the `send_message` alias left the switch with two cases, below the rule's threshold, so the rule no longer fires and the directive became an unused-disable error. It is deleted. The reasoning above stands and the suppression should come back with it the moment a third case is added - which the add-a-message-type how-to walks a reader straight into.

**`re-lint/test-imports-its-subject` on the layering test** (`scripts/eslint-layers.test.ts`). The rule reports that the file loads no first-party module and so cannot fail when production code changes. It does exercise the real `eslint.config.mjs` - through `spawnSync`, because loading a flat config in-process needs `--experimental-vm-modules` - and the rule cannot see through a subprocess. The file exists because the layering gate's failure mode is silence: `no-cross-layer-import` keys packages by `<package>/src/`, so a misconfigured root matches nothing, reports nothing and looks adopted, which is exactly the state this repo was in until it was probed. Deleting or rewriting the test to satisfy the rule removes the only thing that would notice.

## Rationale

A suppression is honest when the rule's premise is false for the site, and dishonest when it is merely inconvenient. Each of these four fails the rule's premise: the "function" is a public constructor, the "dispatch" is a loading boundary, the "dispatch" is a type narrowing, and the "test that loads nothing real" loads the config under test in another process. In each case the rule's suggested remedy is a change that a reviewer would reject on its merits.

Per-site suppression with a written reason was preferred over disabling any rule repo-wide, because three of the four rules have genuine findings elsewhere that should keep failing. `no-flag-params` reports four other sites, `prefer-polymorphism` one, and both counts should fall.

## Consequences

- Five findings no longer appear across the four decisions; two of the three rules keep firing elsewhere.
- A future reader who removes a suppression sees the reason in the `--` clause before deciding.
- The suppressions are load-bearing in one direction: if `AIError` is ever redesigned through the breaking-change process, or the provider factory becomes async, the corresponding suppression should be reconsidered rather than carried forward.
- `re-lint/no-forwarding-class` remains enabled and inert for an unrelated reason - it needs type information this config does not provide - and is documented at its site in `eslint.config.mjs`, not here.

## Alternatives considered

**Refactor to satisfy each rule.** Rejected: a breaking API change outside the documented process, an eager-loading regression, a lost narrowing at a trust boundary, and a deleted anti-silence pin.

**Disable the three rules repo-wide.** Rejected: the suppressions are per-site and visible, and each names its reason. Turning the rules off would silence them for code not yet written, which is where their value is.

**Leave all four failing.** Rejected: a gate that reports findings nobody intends to act on trains readers to ignore it, and these four would never be acted on.

content: I have addressed the linting errors reported by CI

on the last push.

The previous round refactored `validateMessage` into a lookup table (`validators`), which caused
`eslint` to trigger the `camelcase` rule on the literal properties `'user_message'` and `'list_sessions'`. More
importantly, that refactor directly contradicted ADR-006, which states that this trust-boundary type narrowing *must* remain a `switch` statement
and provides a specific inline suppression for the `prefer-polymorphism` rule when the `switch` is extended to a third

case.

I have restored the `switch` statement for `message.type` and added the `eslint-disable

-next-line` directive exactly as prescribed by ADR-006. The code is committed, formatted, and pushed.
